title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
raw_text:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data? AlloyDB Omni , Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere. Built-in AI for your local environment AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment. Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8 . No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance. Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet. title: How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI
raw_text: As the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch , one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages. Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery . Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture The challenge: untangling distributed warehouses and escalating spikes Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points: Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management. Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity. High-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL. “Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.” Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch Phase 1: validating architecture with a target MVP To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework: A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity. Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach — migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts. Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows , which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead. Re-engineering for scale: key architectural pillars 1. Decoupled storage and optimized ingestion Sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sitch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50. For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy. 2. AI-assisted SQL and macro translation In order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how: The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access. Sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates. Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations. Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC ), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision. “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.” Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch Real-world business impact By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth: Metric / capability Before (Snowflake) After (BigQuery) Pipeline performance High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records Compute and billing efficiency Unpredictable month-end billing spikes Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling AI readiness Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform Looking ahead With its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation. By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the company to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

title: CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
raw_text: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform. “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement. The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added. The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk , both completed earlier this year. From partnership to one platform CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said. Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.” The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.” Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach. One contract, one renewal The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. “Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said. Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time. “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate. Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added. Two layers, one release train CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said. For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said. “A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.” Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.” Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
raw_text: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense. Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas. “What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with. “This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers. When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient. “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.” The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.” Take care of business Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work. The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains. Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with. Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.” Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says. Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time. Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable. Challenge your policies and content At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries. “You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted. Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.” Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.” “You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on. “It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had. Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do. “Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.” The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. Embrace deep inspection Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests tailoring an AI prompt to take aim at AI prompts themselves, noting that perhaps the most important capability is a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent. “CISOs should be able to determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service, but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky—such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access,” he says, adding that as AI agents become more common, that same inspection and policy model needs to extend beyond human prompts to agent-driven interactions. Tait believes that CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, browser-based access, and APIs. “The goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application, but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services,” he explains. “This also means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.”

title: Digital sovereignty not smart, says The Hague CIO
raw_text:
Policymakers calling for Europe to be as independent of US technology as possible are unrealistic, says the chief information officer of The Hague, the Netherlands’ seat of government.

The Hague, host of the International Criminal Court (ICC), has become a flashpoint for European alarm about US domination of the software, cloud and AI services on which the continent depends.

Speaking in his municipal office four days before the US imposes sanctions on the ICC, Dennis Ravensbergen faces the practical consequences of that alarm. Earlier US sanctions on court officials and judges, in retaliation for investigations of alleged crimes in Afghanistan and Palestine, had already helped rally Europe to the cause of digital sovereignty. The court was forced to take emergency measures to keep operations running if sanctions obliged its predominantly American IT suppliers to pull the plug.

Trump effect

The Trump administration has stoked European indignation and fear with a succession of goading and threats in retaliation for European regulation and taxation of US technology firms.

That indignation and fear landed on Ravensbergen’s desk in January when The Hague’s councillors voted unanimously to make it a priority to establish digital independence “from countries that are partners but may become threats”. A 10-year digital transformation strategy that Ravensbergen had helped architect and put before the council in 2025 gave it insufficient attention, councillors decreed.

They demanded a plan to get “the greatest possible degree of digital independence” from countries on which the city no longer wished to depend. That effectively means the US suppliers on whose systems the city runs.

Ravensbergen already had an extensive transformation programme under way. The i-Visie 2035 strategy that councillors voted on in January envisages digitising public services, re-engineering them around AI and replacing fragmented bespoke systems with standard cloud software. It promises to make The Hague a smart city: a nervous system of sensors on buildings, roads and utilities, with drones and robots doing maintenance and a central system to control it all.

Residents will contribute to urban works and spaces through an interactive digital twin. There will be wholesale process re-engineering and retraining for 13,000 staff. Cyber security found wanting by independent audits is to be repaired, data standardised and integrated, and systems joined with those of the other three largest Dutch cities, the G4. Microsoft is a supplier of choice.

The sovereignty mandate complicated that transformation. Requiring independence from foreign suppliers was like “changing the course of an oil tanker before the harbour is built”, Ravensbergen and the municipal executive wrote in June. They argued that European alternatives were unavailable because the EU had been more concerned with regulating technology than building it. Change would take years and the alternatives would not be equivalent. Still, the executive agreed to pursue it.

“That’s not really Smart, is it?” Ravensbergen says of the “as sovereign as possible” mandate. “That’s not specific, measurable, acceptable, realistic, time-bound [Smart]. Because how sovereign is sovereign? When is it sovereign enough? Do you only want to have products from Europe? But we don’t have all products from Europe yet.”

Working it out

Policymakers and executives are still working those questions out, he says, even nationally. The G4 were doing studies ahead of another debate at the end of the year. Politicians, he says, are struggling with the question too.

Why, then, had sovereignty not been a priority when i-Visie appeared in September 2025, just four months before the January vote?

“Because the world has changed,” says Ravensbergen. Two or three years ago, replacing on-premise systems with US cloud services had seemed logical. Now, concern about autonomy is growing exponentially.

Pressed on what has changed, he says it is not for the better. Pressed again, he adds that it was Donald Trump’s return to the US presidency in January 2025, which caused pressure for digital sovereignty to grow.

“From that moment on, I was getting more questions about this. From my organisation, from people on the street, at birthday parties, from people [when] you go to a seminar or an event.”

Where once much that came from the US was trusted, now people discuss it – the US had stoked concerns people had already about other countries. “Unfortunately, you cannot trust anybody in the world nowadays,” says Ravensbergen.

He nevertheless agrees that digital independence is a distraction from the things he would rather be doing: delivering useful IT services to the citizens of the city, and especially those who really need municipal help.

Asked why the US cannot be trusted, Ravensbergen laughs. A long, searching pause follows. His PR assistant mumbles something. “It’s, it’s, it’s, it’s, it’s, erm ...” says Ravensbergen.

He then states that the municipality has never had an issue with a US company “or whatever”, but sovereignty is a public discussion and very much in the news. Then there is the ICC – a rare example, but something the municipality must consider. What other examples show that the US cannot be trusted? “I don’t know them,” Ravensbergen says as he laughs. “That’s the most funny thing, isn’t it?”

He adds that risk is an equation: probability times impact. The odds of US sanctions against The Hague are not very big, but the impact would be.

The Hague, a self-styled “international city of peace and justice”, hosts numerous other courts and tribunals besides the ICC, as well as the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, a clutch of NATO agencies, and Europol.

Just as Ravensbergen has been trying, “with great difficulty”, he says, to keep Chinese hardware out of the component supply chains of the municipality’s datacentres, councillors want the same for US systems. The US has meanwhile appeared to be trying to drive its suppliers out of the ICC’s technology supply chain, using dependence on its technology as a geopolitical weapon.

The ICC consolidated its systems on US suppliers after a major cyber security breach in 2023. The US sanctions on its staff later showed how technological dependence made the court vulnerable to political interference. US cloud providers gave the court three days’ notice that services would stop, Giler tells the conference, with Microsoft its primary supplier at the time.

The ICC subsequently cut dependence on US and affiliated suppliers almost in half. A cessation of IT services would halt court proceedings, witness protection schemes and field operations investigating war crimes. Alternatives were limited because the sanctions had a “chilling effect” on other suppliers.

The Council of Europe reported that suppliers “over-complying” with sanctions and over-reliance on Microsoft were the ICC’s problems. For Ravensbergen, the municipality’s dependence on US suppliers remains an operational necessity. The Hague is “very much dependent” on them. It needs them to keep services running.

“It’s part of the job of a CIO to find a balance. Those are my suppliers, and I have good relations with most of them. On average, they’re delivering quite good products that we are very happy to use, that help us deliver good services to the citizens of the municipality of The Hague.”

He has no plans to abandon Microsoft Azure or 365, although the G4 has agreed to test whether Amsterdam municipality’s home-grown AI assistant can replace Copilot. His department mapped 29 major US suppliers and possible substitutes.

“Not that many things are being produced in and by European countries. So, there’s no alternative, both in quantity and quality, to a lot of products that come from outside Europe. What you want is one thing, but what is available is another,” says Ravensbergen.

For now, The Hague is classifying processes, data and systems to determine which are sensitive enough to require a more autonomous platform, using a methodology the G4 developed. It is looking for European alternatives that might become viable in years to come, if not now. Plans to migrate services to US clouds are meanwhile proceeding.

“The discussion we’re having internally is about what kind of data do [we] want to keep in what place,” Ravensbergen says. “Financial or medical data or more sensitive data, we want to have preferably on a European platform. It’s not that we want to get rid of the American suppliers, but we want to think about what kind of products we want to use for what kind of data.

“And that’s going to result in, hopefully, in the next couple of years, the development of a more European market where more IT products and services come available so that we can choose [and so] that we can switch,” he says.

Dutch national policy and the European Commission’s technology sovereignty package take a similar approach. The European Commission proposed building European alternatives, rather than purging foreign suppliers. Sovereignty means the option to choose – it starts with mapping dependencies and risks. Ravensbergen is particularly worried about technology from states running offensive cyber programmes.

EU tech sovereignty chief Henna Virkkunen insisted before the European Parliament that the sovereignty package was not protectionist, but Dutch technology companies have called for it to be so. The package itself offered patches for a failed single market that has left the European tech industry weak. Meanwhile, the European Commission’s programme of single market repair is ongoing.

title: Nation-state APTs don't need new tricks; the old ones still work
raw_text:
Nation-state cyber espionage is a persistent challenge for businesses, particularly as geopolitical tensions grow and new technologies create opportunities for attackers. However, while nation-state groups have demonstrated an ability to exploit technological innovation, this does not mean they are abandoning established intrusion techniques.

Instead, these actors repeatedly demonstrate their sophistication by adapting individual stages of the attack lifecycle to take advantage of new technologies and practices as they become widely adopted and trusted. We've seen this through the abuse of remote working practices, QR codes, device-code authentication, encrypted messaging platforms, legitimate remote-access technologies and, more recently, generative artificial intelligence.

The significance lies less in the novelty of the technology and more in how quickly attackers identify its operational value. As organisations adopt new technologies and processes, nation-state actors assess them in parallel for opportunities to improve initial access, persistence, concealment, social engineering or intelligence collection.

Meanwhile, established techniques such as phishing, credential theft, exploitation of internet-facing vulnerabilities and trusted relationships remain effective and commonplace. What distinguishes nation-state groups is their ability to combine proven attack methods with the resources, time and funding to experiment with emerging technologies.

Treating espionage as a business risk

Cyber espionage conducted or enabled by nation-state actors is as much a business risk as any technical security problem. Organisations must identify which data, systems, relationships and capabilities might hold strategic value to a foreign state, understand the consequences of their compromise and prioritise mitigation accordingly. This is similar to a crown jewels assessment, but framed around what might be valuable to a foreign government rather than simply what is most critical to the organisation.

The C-suite and board don't necessarily need to understand individual threat groups or their techniques. Their responsibility is to ensure ownership, decision-making authority, escalation routes and external relationships are established before an incident occurs. This includes knowing which government departments or law enforcement agencies to contact, understanding regulatory obligations, maintaining reliable records of critical decisions and establishing secure, out-of-band communications.

These arrangements should be tested regularly. Incidents involving Medibank, Optus, Synnovis and Norsk Hydro demonstrate why seemingly mundane preparations around escalation, communications and manual procedures can prove critical during a crisis.

  • Rik Ferguson, Rapid7: Exposing state threats still matters: resilience matters more.

Navigating geopolitical uncertainty

Prolonged geopolitical tensions create another challenge for businesses. Governments can simultaneously pursue economic engagement, diplomatic relations and national security competition with the same state, leaving private organisations to navigate the implications themselves. Businesses may interpret diplomatic or commercial engagement as evidence of reduced security risk, while security warnings suggest they should exercise greater caution.

This creates uncertainty around espionage exposure, supply-chain disruption, regulatory change and political intervention, often driven by circumstances beyond an organisation's control. Relationships that remain commercially attractive and legally valid may still carry strategic risk as the geopolitical environment changes.

Ultimately, boards must translate these competing considerations into their organisation's risk appetite, determining where foreign relationships create tolerable dependencies and where exposure becomes disproportionate.

Nation-state actors have the time, resources and motivation to pursue their objectives persistently. For businesses, the priority must therefore be understanding what makes them strategically valuable targets, preparing for potential compromise and ensuring geopolitical risk is treated as an ongoing board-level responsibility.

title: Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia with backing from Trump
raw_text:
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO of AI chip maker Nvidia in a surprise move following his resignation over a series of extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed by US intelligence officers to be a Chinese spy.

The move follows discussions with senior members of the US government, and a series of meetings with Huang following his resignation on 12 November, that have persuaded Nvidia’s board that Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

US president Donald Trump said in a social media post that reappointing Huang was the correct and proper decision. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he wrote.

Nvidia said in a statement that it believed Huang was the right person to lead the company and that his reinstatement was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, partners and customers, following a unanimous vote by Nvidia’s board.

Harvey Jones, who was appointed chair of Nvidia’s board after Jensen’s resignation said: “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company.”

Huang stood down after it emerged that he had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive linked to the Singapore-based Nvidia customer, Megaspeed, which came under investigation by the US commerce department last year following claims of suspicious activity and the potential diversion of high-end chips in violation of US export law.

US intelligence officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited as a Chinese spy by China’s Ministry of State Security.

Huang, who has provided $25m of financial support to Trump’s controversial White House ballroom project, has been a vocal campaigner for the US to allow more exports of advanced AI chips produced by Nvidia to China.

The CEO is known for his hands-on approach to running Nvidia, managing 60 direct reports, and intervening in every aspect of the company’s strategy and technology development.

Nvidia said it had formed a committee of independent directors and independent legal counsel to investigate reports that Jensen Huang has been targeted by Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang supported the investigation and was co-operating with it.

The company has set up a national security and export control committee, made up of independent directors to oversee trade, compliance and national security risks, and plans to appoint advisers with expertise in national security. The company also plans to appoint a chief compliance officer in a move to improve corporate governance.

Jensen Huang said: “I am honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.”

He expressed his gratitude to Nvidia chair Jones, interim CEO Colette Kress, and Nvidia’s executive team for leading the company.

“I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

Jones, who will remain as chair of the board, said he was grateful to Kress, who returns to being Nvidia’s chief financial officer, after she stood in as interim CEO following Huang’s initial departure.

title: Britain’s data sharing plans should be judged by who they help
raw_text:
Since February, every petrol station in the UK has had to report pump price changes within 30 minutes. The prices go into a free government feed that comparison apps and sat navs use to show drivers the cheapest fuel nearby, and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) reckons that shopping around can save up to £9 on a tank of fuel. Most commentators have treated Fuel Finder as a cost-of-living measure, with few mentioning that it is an early scheme in a much larger government programme.

That programme is called “smart data,” and it covers two kinds of information. The first is business information like prices and locations, published openly so that app developers can build services with it, as they now do with pump prices. The second is personal records, which a company passes onto another provider of the customer’s choosing, with their permission. The Data (Use and Access) Act lets ministers extend this approach to energy, property, transport and retail, and the government wants at least twenty schemes running by 2035. The call for evidence on which sectors will come next closed in early October; however, a target counted on schemes says little about whether people will use them.

In the 2010s, a voluntary scheme called midata let bank customers download their account history as a spreadsheet, in the hope they would use it to find better deals. Few people wanted to download spreadsheets of their own spending and then upload them to comparison sites, and the CMA later found that usage was very low. A few banks, including HSBC and Santander, still offer the download option, but most people now share their banking data through open banking, making the manual process largely redundant. The right to share the data had existed for years, but almost no one used it until it became much easier.

  • Why open data is needed in the battle to address homelessness: Centrepoint needed to send FOIs to more than 300 local authorities in England to access required information.

Open banking made sharing automatic when it arrived in 2018 through an EU payments law, PSD2, which required banks to let licensed firms access customer accounts with permission, and a CMA order that made Britain’s largest banks build common standards for doing so. Even so, the mass switching of current accounts that regulators anticipated never happened. Instead, people took up open banking through budgeting apps and challenger banks such as Monzo, which gave them good reasons to share, and it now has more than 17 million users.

However, a legal right and working technology still do not guarantee use, as Australia found out after legislating a data right covering its whole economy in 2019. It launched a scheme in banking, where customers could share data but not act on it, for example, by moving money or switching accounts. A review by the Australian Treasury found that strict limits on sharing the data held back new services from developing. By 2023, according to research by the country’s banks, only 0.31% of customers were using it, after the industry had spent around A$1.5 billion.

Brazil’s banking customers had a very different experience. The country’s central bank made participation compulsory for the largest institutions and tied data sharing to Pix (the instant payment system millions of people already used) from the beginning. By September this year, Brazil had counted 269 million active data sharing consents.

The UK’s Fuel Finder follows similar principles on a small scale, since every forecourt has to take part and the prices reach drivers through apps they already use. Registration has reached around 97% of petrol stations so far. Its weak point has been data quality, with What Car?  reporting that several apps showed out-of-date prices that could leave regular users up to £260 a year worse off. Whether it has brought prices down for consumers overall will be clear only when the CMA reports this autumn.

What this tells us is that the next schemes will need compulsory participation, accurate data, and a route to people through services they already use. Home buying is a good candidate, with buyers and sellers already relying on conveyancers and estate agents to chase documents (often in interminable circles) between councils, lenders and the Land Registry. A scheme that compels these bodies to share verified records would reach people through companies they already use, and costly delays in buying and selling property give consumers a reason to want it. A digital property pack from Moverly and the Open Property Data Association, which won the Smart Data Challenge Prize, shows what such a scheme could do. However, it has so far been tested only on synthetic data, but in October, the Open Property Coalition announced that it will test digital property IDs and ways to share property data securely.

Unlike Fuel Finder, schemes in most other sectors will rely on a trade in which customers share their records for faster decisions and/or cheaper products. The government is already consulting on rules that would require energy companies to share certain data with authorised services when customers choose to share it. The risk is that sharing becomes compulsory in name only.

A lender, insurer or energy supplier does not have to refuse customers who keep their data private if it can simply charge them more, reserving its best prices for those who hand over their records. People who can afford the higher price will keep their privacy, and everyone else will pay with their data.

The government’s strategy sets aside one per cent of the smart data budget for monitoring and evaluation, mainly to track growth. As the ODI urged in our response to the recent smart data consultation, it should also show who benefits by publishing how many people use each scheme, what they save and who is charged more for declining to share. Fuel Finder asks drivers for nothing, and there are no penalties for ignoring it. Every scheme should meet the same standard: people use services because they get a better deal, and there are no punitive consequences for saying “no.”

Josh D’Addario is head of consultancy, the Open Data Institute (ODI), which is a member of the UK Smart Data Council.
summary:
Since February, every petrol station in the UK has had to report pump price changes within 30 minutes. The prices go into a free government feed that comparison apps and sat navs use to show drivers the cheapest fuel nearby, and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) reckons that shopping around can save up to £9 on a tank of fuel. Most commentators have treated Fuel Finder as a cost-of-living measure, with few mentioning that it is an early scheme in a much larger government programme.

That programme is called “smart data,” and it covers two kinds of information. The first is business information like prices and locations, published openly so that app developers can build services with it, as they now do with pump prices.

title: UK Sovereign AI Fund invests in defence tech startup
raw_text:
The UK government’s Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) have invested in Agon, a company developing the infrastructure needed to train, validate and orchestrate autonomous defence systems. Among the infrastructure the company hopes to develop are artificial intelligence (AI) tools that are designed to defend against drone attacks, as well as a way to ensure AI continues to work as intended if communications are disrupted by an adversary.

Agon is also building a “virtual battlefield” where AI models can be tested cost-effectively against realistic simulations of the situations they might encounter.

The Sovereign AI fund is part of a wider government effort to support British AI innovators and founders to help them develop capabilities that would enable the UK to avoid being too heavily reliant on technology from overseas providers. The National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) invests in dual-use technologies that strengthen the UK’s national security and defence.

By backing innovative companies developing strategically important capabilities, the government said NSSIF helps enhance the nation’s security, resilience and technological advantage. It said the investment in Agon reflects a continued commitment to technologies with clear national security relevance and the potential to deliver lasting impact.

Agon is one of a number of companies being supported to develop and support home-grown technology and AI capabilities.

Junaid Hussain, co-founder of Agon, said: “Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend. Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety.”

During the Autumn Budget, the chancellor announced an additional £140m backing for the Sovereign AI Fund. The chancellor also announced that sovereign AI would expand into a new focus area of physical and industrial AI, building on the UK’s leading research base and growing strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

Sovereign AI investor Will Bushby said: “Defence AI is too important to leave to others. It’s not enough for the UK and Europe to be able to deploy this technology, we need to be able to build it too.”

Discussing the investment, AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era.

“Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure these technologies are reliable, trustworthy and deployed responsibly. Agon’s work will make a valuable contribution to this work: not just British-made AI that our military can use to keep us safe, but defence AI that’s been built in the right way.”

Tristam Constant, co-founder and CEO of Agon, said: “Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match. We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities.”

Based in London and with a second office in Berlin, the company has raised a total of $100m to date.

title: Staff gagging clauses lifted for review of ‘toxic culture’ at information watchdog
raw_text:
Current and former staff of the UK’s information watchdog the Information Commission’s Office (ICO) will have non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) lifted to allow them to contribute to an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance at the organisation.

The review follows the resignation of the information commissioner, John Edwards, in June following allegations of sexual harassment and bullying, leaving a gap in the organisation’s senior leadership that has yet to be filled.

Edwards acknowledged that his conduct fell below the high standards required of leaders in public life, saying there were occasions when “he exercised poor judgement” and had “made attempts at humour that were inappropriate”.

The Information Commission is responsible for regulating data protection and freedom of information and has issued more than £17m fines over the past year, including a £12m fine against TikTok for data protection breaches, including failures to lawfully use children’s data.

Ministers, as first reported by the BBC, are expected to announce details of an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance at the Information Commission this week.

Internal problems

Multiple ICO sources have told Computer Weekly that the regulator’s internal problems extended beyond Edwards to the wider senior leadership at the Information Commission, who were aware of Edwards’ conduct but failed to protect staff.

The Information Commission has entered into 16 non-disclosure agreements with current or former members of staff at a cost of £354,000 since January 2020, according to  disclosures under the Freedom of Information Act (FoI). Nine of the agreements included clauses to prevent employees making disparaging comments about their former employer.

Lawrence Dunne, industrial officer at the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS), speaking on the BBC’s Today programme on Saturday, said that he hoped the lifting of the NDA’s would allow the review to get at the truth.

“It’s something that PCS has been calling for consistently for some time – that the voice of both the current and former ICO staff who have been the victim of a toxic culture for too long are heard, so we can get to the full truth of the extent of the issues that have been going on,” he added.

He said that compared to other government departments, the Information Commission had issued a large number of NDA agreements. “It really is disturbing that we found that so many have been signed over such a short period of time,” he added.

Staff experienced bullying and harassment

Computer Weekly previously reported that an ICO staff survey this year found that almost one in four employees had experienced or witnessed bullying, harassment or discrimination in the previous 12 months, with more than a third of the incidents involving senior staff. Only 34% of employees said they felt safe speaking up or challenging the way things are done in the organisation.

Following Edward’s resignation, the former technology secretary, Liz Kendall, announced on 8 July that the government would launch an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance of the Information Commission.

Wynne Parry, National Officer at the FDA union, which represents managers and professionals in the public sector, said that the union had been pressing for the independent review since Kendall’s announcement.

“The review needs to be truly independent if it is to gain the confidence of the Commission staff, and the investigation needs to be able to speak freely with those who wish to bring their experience forward,” he added. “We welcome the decision to lift gagging orders so that current and ex-staff can contribute.”

Review should look at resources

Ken Macdonald, former head of ICO Regions, told Computer Weekly that lifting NDA restrictions may be uncomfortable for long-serving members of the existing leadership team but was a necessary step.

“I’m delighted that the gags are to be lifted and, with the implication from that, that former members of staff will be able to feed into the investigation. For them not to would only diminish the investigation’s findings, but the lifting of the non-derogatory elements of NDAs could bring a whole new dimension to the investigation,” he added.

Macdonald said that management and administrative layers in the Information Commission had grown leaving fewer resources for the Information Commission’s core regulatory work.  

“The case backlogs alone tell a story and make a mockery of even the softest of regulatory actions being taken when the Commission isn’t meeting regulatory requirements itself,” he said. “An independent root-and-branch review of its corporate structures is needed and should follow the initial investigation.”

He said that he was concerned that resources for the ICO’s work in the regions had been reduced, with the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish public affairs teams having to manage with fewer staff.

Vulgar and sexualised language

Following Edward’s resignation, former technology secretary Kendall wrote in a post on LinkedIn that an internal investigation had found that the information commissioner’s conduct had fallen short of the standards expected.

“I have seen evidence of the vulgar and highly sexualised language that was used in his interactions with his staff and am extremely concerned that he continues to describe these incidents as misplaced humour,” she said in the statement. “Multiple women shared testimony to the investigator on feeling offended, shocked and uncomfortable following interactions with Mr Edwards.”

A spokesperson from the Department of Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees the Information Commission, confirmed that the watchdog will not use the terms of any non-disclosure agreements to prevent people from participating in the review.

“An independent review of culture, accountability and governance at the Information Commission is going ahead. We will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly,” the spokesperson added.

ICO ‘committed to learning’

The Information Commission said that it was committed to listening and learning from the events of the past years.

A spokesperson said: “We have never used confidentiality agreements to silence anybody from speaking out about bullying or harassment and we will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the upcoming independent review.

“John Edwards’s conduct was unacceptable and fell well short of the standards we expect, and of the safe, respectful working environment every member of staff deserves. Our new noard, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy. It is committed to listening carefully to the review’s findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation.”

The organisation was restructured on 2 October to bring it in line with other regulators, with responsibility for making decisions now being vested in a board, rather than an individual commissioner.

The Information Commission appointed seven non-executive members in July 2026, who will now play a role in the organisation’s governance strategy.

The regulator is in the process of appointing a new chair, who is expected to take up post in spring 2027.

title: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez resigns over botched contract
raw_text:
Capita’s CEO will not get to fix the company’s Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) work as he steps down as a consequence of the botched contract.

The company’s share price tanked on news of profits falling by over 50% on Monday 23 November. Extra Capita spending related to trying to fix the CSPS will see profits reduced by over £90m, the firm said.

Capita’s heavy reliance on the UK public sector, combined with its mistakes on the CSPS and the current government’s policy to insource more business, will put the company under pressure.

Adolfo Hernandez, who has had to face public scrutiny as a result of Capita’s disastrous running of the CSPS, will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres.

Hernandez earned £1.6m in his last pay packet, while thousands of retired civil servants on a pension scheme run by Capita were, as a result of its mistakes, forced to apply for emergency loans.

Capita said in a statement: “The board and Adolfo Hernandez have agreed that Adolfo will step down as CEO and as a member of the board with immediate effect.”

One CSPS member said: “There are interesting reactions on Facebook. Most are elated [that Hernandez is going] but a few are concerned about the risks if Capita collapses completely.”

Hernandez criticised internally

In August, as revealed by Computer Weekly, Hernandez was slammed via an internal message board after making claims that the “right” things are in place to turn the CSPS administration around. The comments from a staff member cast doubt on Capita’s ability to fix the problems being experienced by members of the pension scheme.

In a response to a Hernandez statement, copied to all Capita staff, a member of the pensions team said: “The service provided by Capita surpasses your assertion of ‘not good enough’, it has been abysmal for members. The fact members have died in waiting due to this whole catastrophe is a really harrowing thought that none of us should have to live with, yet we sadly do.”

The worker said that staff have been trying to air their concerns about the CSPS contract, but that all contacts have been “met with vague, deflective and meaningless responses”.

Former civil servant and CSPS member Steve Tessier said: “Glad to see that there is at least some accountability at last.”

Pointing towards the Cabinet Office’s role in the pension scheme disaster, he added: “There are plenty of others who should be getting a P45, too, and not just people from Capita.”

Reacting to Hernandez’s exit, the Civil Service Campaigns Group, made up of people affected by pension delays, said: “Hernandez was CEO throughout this crisis and must be held accountable for Capita’s failures. We repeatedly raised serious concerns directly with him and his senior leadership team, including the devastating impact on members, yet saw little evidence of meaningful action.

“His departure must not be allowed to draw a line under these failures. He, Capita’s board and the Cabinet Office must be held to account for what went wrong, why repeated warnings were ignored and the harm caused to members.”

It added that its “immediate concern is ensuring Capita’s financial difficulties do not further destabilise the service or disrupt pension payments”.

“Changing the CEO does not remove responsibility for what happened on his watch,” the Civil Service Campaigns Group said.

Pension disaster

In 2023, the Cabinet Office awarded Capita a seven-year contract worth £239m for the administration of the CSPS, which has 1.7 million members. The takeover from the previous administrator, MyCSP, took place on 1 December 2025. 

Since it took on the contract, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises, leaving claimants in severe financial difficulties. Thousands of retired civil servants are affected by the CSPS problems – some have waited nearly a year for their pensions, and at least one has been forced to use a food bank.

Capita has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on the organisation, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

In January 2026, just a month after Capita took over from MyCSP and following a litany of problems, a troubleshooter stepped in from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to lead an “urgent recovery plan”, which included 150 staff being moved temporarily from HMRC to the service.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house, but no timeline has been given.
